title: Strategy and Research Function in a Life Insurance Company

blocks.h: On completing this chapter, the reader should be able to:

items.h: Explain the role of the strategy function in a life insurance company, describe how strategic planning connects to financial management, governance, and operational decisions, and identify the principal outputs of a well-designed strategic planning process.

Apply the PESTEL framework to the Nigerian life insurance environment, analysing the political, economic, social, technological, environmental, and legal factors shaping the strategic landscape for Nigerian life insurers in the post-NIIRA 2025 era.

Apply Porter’s Five Forces model to competitive analysis in the Nigerian life insurance sector, evaluating the bargaining power of buyers and suppliers, the threat of new entrants and substitutes, and the intensity of competitive rivalry.

Describe the components of a competitive strategy for a Nigerian life insurer (cost leadership, differentiation, and focus strategies) and explain how each translates into specific choices about product range, distribution, pricing, and positioning.

Describe the market research and consumer insights function of a life insurance company, explain the primary and secondary research methods most appropriate for the Nigerian insurance market, and identify the research outputs that feed directly into product development, pricing, and marketing strategy.

Explain the structured product innovation process in life insurance, from market insight through concept development, actuarial design, regulatory filing, pilot testing, and full launch, and describe NAICOM’s role in product approval.

Describe the digital strategy framework for a Nigerian life insurer, including the role of Insurtech, digital distribution, data analytics, and AI in the insurance value chain, and explain NAICOM’s Insurtech regulatory sandbox.

Describe the Balanced Scorecard framework as applied to life insurance strategic performance management, and explain how OKRs (Objectives and Key Results) can complement the Balanced Scorecard for agile strategy execution.

Explain the concept of strategic risk, the risk that the strategy itself is wrong or poorly executed, and describe the governance mechanisms required to identify, monitor, and respond to strategic risk in a life insurance context.

Describe the design of a research function within a Nigerian life insurance company, including its mandate, team structure, data sources, research agenda, and the mechanisms for translating research outputs into strategic and product decisions.

blocks.text: 27.1 Introduction: The Strategic Imperative for Nigerian Life Insurers

blocks.h: Strategy is the insurer’s theory of how it will win in its market. It is not a document, a planning meeting, or a PowerPoint deck. It is a set of choices (about which customers to serve, which products to offer, which distribution channels to invest in, which capabilities to build, and which competitors to outmanoeuvre) that, taken together, create a distinctive and defensible competitive position. An insurer without a deliberate strategy does not have no strategy; it has a default strategy, which is to do what everyone else does, charge similar prices, and hope for a larger share of a slow-growing market.

The Nigerian life insurance market in 2025 and beyond demands deliberate strategy for several reasons. First, the market is at an inflection point: NIIRA 2025’s capital consolidation requirements, the rise of Insurtech distribution, the demographic bulge of 15–35-year-old digital-native Nigerians, and the mandatory insurance extensions are simultaneously creating competitive threats and growth opportunities that did not exist five years ago. Second, the market’s long-term potential, a country of 220+ million people with insurance penetration below 0.5% of GDP, is large enough to support multiple competing growth strategies. Third, the capital requirements of NIIRA 2025 mean that strategic mistakes are more expensive: an insurer that builds the wrong distribution infrastructure or enters the wrong product segment in a post-consolidation market may not have the capital to correct course.

This chapter builds on the financial management, governance, and distribution knowledge accumulated across Parts Three to Five to address the strategic and research questions that define the Nigerian life insurer’s competitive future: how to analyse the environment, how to position the business, how to generate the consumer and market insights that drive innovation, how to execute through digital channels, how to measure strategic progress, and how to build the research and intelligence infrastructure that makes strategy continuously informed rather than periodically guessed.
A well-designed strategic planning process translates the insurer’s purpose and vision into specific, actionable choices and measurable targets. It has five sequential stages:

items.h: Environmental scanning: Understanding the external environment (PESTEL and competitive analysis) to identify the opportunities and threats that define the strategic landscape.
Internal assessment: Evaluating the insurer’s own capabilities, resources, and competitive position; the honest assessment of what the organisation can do well relative to its competitors.

Strategic choice: Making deliberate, prioritised decisions about the competitive position the insurer will pursue, which markets, products, channels, and customer segments to focus on, and which to avoid.

Strategic translation: Converting the strategic choice into an operating plan: the investment priorities, the organisational changes, the product development roadmap, the distribution build, and the financial targets for the next 3–5 years.
Performance management: Establishing the metrics, targets, review cadence, and governance mechanisms that hold the organisation accountable for strategy execution.

blocks.text: 27.2.2 The Annual vs. Long-Horizon Strategy Cycle

blocks.h: Strategic planning operates at two temporal scales simultaneously: the annual budget cycle (addressed in Chapter 26), which sets the financial targets for the next 12 months; and the long-horizon strategy review (typically conducted every 3 years), which reassesses the fundamental choices about the insurer’s competitive position. These two cycles must be synchronised: the annual budget should be the first year of the long-horizon strategy, not a stand-alone financial exercise disconnected from strategic direction.

In the context of the Nigerian market’s current transformation (NIIRA 2025, consolidation, Insurtech, demographic change) a 3-year horizon strategy review conducted in 2025 would look radically different from one conducted in 2022. The pace of environmental change in the Nigerian insurance sector argues for more frequent strategy reviews (annually) at a lighter level and a deeper strategic reassessment every three years when the accumulated environmental changes warrant a more fundamental re-evaluation of position.

blocks.text: 27.3 Environmental Scanning: PESTEL Analysis for Nigerian Life Insurance

blocks.h: The PESTEL framework provides a structured approach to scanning the macro-environment for forces that create opportunities and threats for the insurer. Applied to the Nigerian life insurance market in the post-NIIRA 2025 era, PESTEL reveals a landscape of simultaneously enabling and disruptive forces that every strategy function must understand.

rows: PESTEL Factor
Key Forces in Nigerian Life Insurance (2025 and Beyond)
Strategic Implication
Political

NIIRA 2025 capital consolidation (increased minimum capital driving M&A); mandatory insurance extensions (credit life, group life) creating new compulsory demand; government financial inclusion agenda (NFS 2020–2024 successor framework); PenCom reform agenda influencing the annuity market.

Consolidation creates acquisition opportunities for well-capitalised insurers; mandatory insurance creates a structural new premium income floor; financial inclusion agenda legitimises microinsurance investment.
Economic

High nominal interest rates (22%+ MPR environment in 2024–2025) creating attractive short-term investment income but ALM risk; Naira depreciation creating inflation in claims costs and foreign-currency liabilities; strong nominal GDP growth (Sub-Saharan Africa’s largest economy); growing middle class and formal sector employment base; high inflation eroding real premium growth.

High rates accelerate the case for ALM duration extension; Naira depreciation requires foreign-currency asset hedging; middle-class growth is the primary long-term demand driver for individual life products.
Social

Young demographic profile (median age ~18); rising urbanisation (Lagos, Abuja, Enugu, Kano growth); increasing tertiary education levels; growing awareness of financial planning among the urban professional cohort; deep distrust of insurance from historical claim non-payment; strong Ajo/cooperative savings culture in informal communities.

Youth demographics create long-term demand but low immediate premium levels; trust deficit is the primary marketing obstacle; savings culture is the entry point for insurance education and product design.
Technological

Mobile money penetration (80%+ mobile subscribers); Insurtech entrants challenging incumbent distribution models; AI and data analytics enabling granular risk pricing; digital distribution reducing CAC; USSD enabling financial services in feature-phone markets; API integration enabling embedded insurance in fintech and agritech platforms.

Technology-enabled distribution is the biggest opportunity for cost-efficient market expansion; AI pricing may shift competitive advantage from distribution scale to data quality; incumbent insurers must digitise or cede ground to Insurtech entrants.
Environmental

Climate change increasing severity of floods, heat, and drought in Nigeria; agricultural weather risk driving demand for parametric insurance products; ESG investor pressure on listed insurers; NAICOM Green Finance integration initiative encouraging green insurance products.

Climate risk creates new product opportunities (parametric agricultural, flood, climate health); ESG reporting requirements are an emerging governance obligation; green bonds are an increasingly relevant admissible asset class.
Legal

NIIRA 2025 comprehensive regulatory reform (capital, governance, consumer protection, Insurtech, IFRS 17, RBC); NDPA 2023 data protection obligations; MLPPA 2022 AML/CFT requirements; Pension Reform Act 2014 (CPS/annuity market structure); Companies and Allied Matters Act (CAMA) 2020 governance requirements.

NIIRA 2025 is the dominant near-term strategic environment driver; compliance investment is substantial but creates competitive differentiation for early adopters; NDPA 2023 requires data governance infrastructure investment.

blocks.text: 27.4 Competitive Analysis: Porter’s Five Forces in Nigerian Life Insurance

blocks.h: Porter’s Five Forces framework analyses the competitive dynamics of an industry by examining five structural forces that determine the profitability available to incumbents. Applied to Nigerian life insurance, the Five Forces analysis reveals a market where competitive intensity is moderate but rising, and where the most significant structural shifts are occurring in the dimensions of new entrants (Insurtech) and substitute products (informal savings and digital savings platforms).

rows: Force 1: Threat of New Entrants

CURRENTLY MODERATE; RISING RAPIDLY. The NIIRA 2025 minimum capital requirements create a financial barrier to pure greenfield entry. However, the Insurtech licensing framework and the corporate agent model create lower-barrier entry points: a well-funded fintech with a large user base can become a material insurance distributor without holding a full insurance licence. International insurers (pan-African groups such as Sanlam, Old Mutual, and Allianz) have entered or expanded in Nigeria, bringing capital, technical expertise, and brand recognition that domestic incumbents must respond to.
Force 2: Bargaining Power of Buyers

INDIVIDUALLY WEAK; COLLECTIVELY GROWING. Individual retail policyholders have minimal bargaining power; they cannot negotiate pricing or terms and typically have limited ability to compare products. However, digital comparison tools and financial literacy growth are increasing consumer awareness. Corporate buyers (HR directors, CFOs) have significantly higher bargaining power in the group life market, particularly for large schemes where they can invite competitive tenders. The growing broker community amplifies buyer power by aggregating demand.
Force 3: Bargaining Power of Suppliers

MODERATE. The insurer’s primary ‘suppliers’ are its distribution intermediaries (agents, bancassurance banks, brokers), its reinsurers, and its technology providers. Bancassurance banks have significant bargaining power: a bank with a large customer base can negotiate favourable commission terms and may switch insurer partners. International reinsurers have moderate power, the domestic reinsurance market (NRC, Continental Re) provides some local sourcing alternative, but for large programmes, international capacity is necessary.
Force 4: Threat of Substitutes

MODERATE AND GROWING. The primary substitutes for life insurance in the Nigerian market are: informal savings (Ajo/Esusu provides some mutual protection function); digital savings platforms (Piggyvest, Cowrywise); real estate (Nigerians’ preferred long-term wealth storage); and the extended family support network (the traditional Nigerian social insurance system). As digital savings platforms become more sophisticated and offer higher yields than traditional bank savings, their substitution effect on savings-linked insurance products will grow.
Force 5: Competitive Rivalry

MODERATE BUT INTENSIFYING POST-CONSOLIDATION. The Nigerian life insurance market has approximately 25–30 licensed life insurers, but the market is highly concentrated at the top: the top five to seven insurers account for the majority of gross written premium. Post-NIIRA 2025 consolidation will reduce the number of players but increase the scale and financial strength of the survivors. Competition on price is constrained by actuarial pricing requirements and NAICOM oversight, but competition on distribution (bancassurance terms, agent recruitment), product innovation, and brand trust is intensifying.

blocks.text: 27.5 Competitive Strategy for a Nigerian Life Insurer

blocks.h: Michael Porter’s generic strategy framework identifies three sustainable competitive strategies: cost leadership (winning by having the lowest cost base in the market); differentiation (winning by offering distinctive products or services that customers value and are willing to pay a premium for); and focus (winning by serving a specific niche market with either lower cost or superior differentiation than broader competitors). An insurer that tries to pursue all three simultaneously, ‘stuck in the middle’, typically succeeds at none.

rows: Strategy
What It Means in Life Insurance
Capabilities Required
Nigerian Life Insurance Example Context
Cost Leadership
Being the lowest-cost provider of equivalent insurance protection in the market, enabling competitive pricing and superior profit margins at market-rate premiums.
Technology-driven distribution (USSD, digital) to eliminate agent commission; automated underwriting and claims; scale economies from large portfolio; highly efficient operations.

A digital-first insurer using USSD distribution and automated underwriting can price term assurance significantly below agent-distributed incumbents. Requires very large volumes to spread fixed technology costs.
Differentiation

Offering products and services that customers recognise as significantly superior to alternatives (in claims speed, breadth of coverage, financial advisory quality, or digital experience) and are willing to pay a modest premium for.
Brand trust; claims excellence; product innovation capability; advisor quality; digital experience investment; service quality superiority.

A well-capitalised incumbent with a documented claims payment record, strong NPS scores, and an integrated digital-physical service model can charge a modest premium over rivals and attract retention-oriented customers.
Focus: Niche Cost
Targeting a specific segment (e.g., low-income, specific occupation, specific geographic area) and serving it at lower cost than broader competitors.
Deep segment knowledge; tailored distribution partnerships; simplified product range; community relationships.

A microinsurance specialist that builds cooperative partnerships across 500 market associations in the South-West can achieve very low CAC and claim rates in that segment that are uneconomic for a generalist insurer.
Focus: Niche Differentiation

Targeting a specific high-value segment (e.g., HNIs, corporate EB clients, annuity specialists) and serving it with a level of advisory quality and product sophistication that generalist competitors cannot match.
Deep product expertise; senior advisor talent; relationship management systems; bespoke product design capability.

An insurer specialising in HNI and corporate EB with a team of senior financial planning professionals, bespoke estate planning and keyman products, and direct access to international placement capacity.

blocks.text: 27.5.2 The Nigerian Life Insurer’s Strategic Position Assessment

blocks.h: Most Nigerian life insurers currently lack a clearly articulated and internally consistent strategic position. They pursue individual life through agents, group life through brokers and corporate sales teams, bancassurance through multiple bank partnerships, and microinsurance through ad hoc community relationships, without a clear priority among these channels and without a clear position in the mind of any customer segment.

The strategic planning process must force a choice: which customer segments are we going to serve with genuine excellence, and which are we going to exit or serve at minimum viable levels? An insurer that genuinely commits to the corporate EB and HNI segment must invest in talent, product, and service quality at a level that requires reducing investment elsewhere. An insurer that commits to digital-first mass market must invest in technology and automated operations at a level that changes the cost structure of the business. Half-measures in each direction produce mediocrity in all.

The market research function exists to answer questions that cannot be answered by reviewing the insurer’s own financial and operational data. It provides the external intelligence (about consumer behaviour, competitor positioning, market trends, regulatory intentions, and technological developments) that informs both strategic planning and day-to-day business decisions. An insurer that makes strategic and product decisions based solely on its own historical data is reasoning from a rear-view mirror; the research function provides the windshield view.

The research function in a Nigerian life insurer serves four mandates: market sizing and segmentation (how large is each market segment? how is it growing? what are the characteristics of the insurable population in each?); consumer insight generation (what do consumers in each segment understand about insurance? what barriers prevent purchase? what value propositions resonate?); competitive intelligence (what products, pricing, and positioning are competitors deploying? what distribution investments are they making?); and regulatory and environmental tracking (what changes in the NIIRA 2025 implementation landscape, NAICOM supervisory focus, or macroeconomic environment will affect the business?).

blocks.text: 27.6.2 Primary Research Methods for the Nigerian Insurance Market

blocks.h: The choice of research method must be appropriate for the target segment and the question being asked. Nigerian insurance market research has historically relied too heavily on telephone surveys of urban formal-sector samples, producing data that systematically over-represents the already-insured population and under-represents the informal sector, rural, and low-income populations that represent the greatest growth opportunity.

Best For

blocks.text: 27.6.3 Secondary Research Sources for Nigerian Insurance

blocks.h: A well-resourced research function supplements primary research with systematic use of secondary sources. Key secondary research sources for Nigerian life insurance strategy include:

items.h: EFInA Access to Financial Services Survey: The most comprehensive demand-side data on financial services access in Nigeria, conducted every two years. The primary source for market sizing, financial inclusion measurement, and insurance penetration benchmarking.

NAICOM Annual Report and Market Returns: Published regulatory statistics on gross written premium, claims paid, licensed insurer count, and market concentration. The definitive source for market share and competitive benchmarking data.
NBS (National Bureau of Statistics) surveys: Income distribution, household expenditure, occupation, and demographic data. The foundation for market segmentation and affordability analysis.
Swiss Re Sigma and Munich Re publications: Global and African insurance market data; re-insurance pricing trends; emerging risk assessments; technology and innovation benchmarking.

GSMA Mobile Economy Africa report: Mobile money penetration, mobile internet adoption, and digital services usage across Nigeria and comparable African markets. Critical for digital strategy calibration.

blocks.h: Product innovation in life insurance is not a creative exercise detached from commercial reality; it is a structured, cross-functional process that translates consumer insight and market opportunity into commercially viable, actuarially sound, and regulatorily compliant products. The most common failure mode in Nigerian insurance product innovation is not lack of creativity; it is the development of technically interesting products that do not address a genuine consumer need, cannot be distributed at the required cost, or cannot be priced to generate acceptable margins.
A structured product innovation process moves through six sequential gates, each requiring sign-off from the relevant function before the process advances:

GATE 1: CONSUMER INSIGHT AND OPPORTUNITY IDENTIFICATION. What consumer need or market gap has research identified? Is the need large enough (market size), underserved enough (competitive gap), and accessible enough (distribution feasibility) to justify product development? Gate owner: Research/Strategy function. Output: Market Opportunity Assessment.

GATE 2: CONCEPT DEVELOPMENT. What is the product concept? Define the target customer, the core benefit, the premium range, the distribution channel, and the key design principles (simplicity, affordability, accessibility, value visibility for mass market; sophistication, breadth, and advisory quality for HNI). Gate owner: Product Management + Distribution. Output: Product Concept Document.

GATE 3: ACTUARIAL DESIGN AND PRICING. Design the benefit structure, the underwriting approach, and the pricing basis. Calculate the expected profit margin (New Business Margin) and the sensitivity of the margin to variations in the key assumptions (mortality, lapse, investment return, expenses). Gate owner: Actuarial function. Output: Actuarial Technical Note and Pricing Model.

GATE 4: REGULATORY FILING. Prepare the product filing for NAICOM: policy wording, benefit illustration template, premium schedule, distribution channel approval. Obtain NAICOM’s product approval (or deemed approval under NIIRA 2025’s 30-day provision). Gate owner: Compliance/Legal function. Output: NAICOM Product Approval.

GATE 5: PILOT. Launch the product in a controlled pilot: a specific distribution channel, a specific geographic market, or a specific customer segment. Monitor the pilot metrics: enrolment rate, persistency at 90 days, CAC, claims experience, and NPS. Gate owner: Distribution + Research. Output: Pilot Assessment Report.

GATE 6: FULL LAUNCH. Based on pilot results, decide: full launch (if metrics meet targets), pivot (if specific design elements need modification), or kill (if the product concept is fundamentally flawed). A product that fails at pilot stage is a learning investment; a product that is fully launched without pilot validation and then fails at scale is a capital destruction event. Gate owner: Executive Committee. Output: Launch Decision and Full Commercial Plan.

A digital strategy for a life insurer is not a technology plan; it is a business strategy that uses technology as its primary enabler. The distinction matters: a technology plan answers ‘what systems should we build?’; a digital strategy answers ‘how will technology change the way we acquire customers, service policyholders, assess risk, and manage claims, and how does that change our competitive position?’.
The digital strategy framework for a Nigerian life insurer has four interconnected dimensions:

rows: Digital Distribution

Using digital channels (mobile app, USSD, insurer website, social media, fintech and agritech platform integrations) as the primary or supplementary distribution infrastructure. Digital distribution reduces CAC by eliminating or supplementing agent commissions, enables 24/7 customer access, and reaches populations geographically inaccessible to physical distribution. The investment required: digital platform development, digital lead generation, and the agent app that enables hybrid phygital distribution.
Digital Servicing

Enabling policyholders to manage their policies, make payments, update beneficiaries, check balances, and initiate claims through digital self-service channels. Digital servicing reduces contact centre cost, improves policyholder engagement frequency, and creates the interaction data from which consumer insights can be derived. The investment required: customer portal, mobile app, WhatsApp Business integration, and back-office process automation.
Data Analytics and AI

Using policyholder data, claims data, market data, and third-party data to: improve risk selection and underwriting accuracy; detect claims fraud earlier; personalise product offers and renewal interactions; and predict lapse risk so that conservation interventions can be targeted precisely. The investment required: data infrastructure (data warehouse, CRM, PAS integration), analytics talent, and AI/ML model development.
Digital Operations

Automating the insurer’s core operational processes: underwriting decisioning (automated approval for standard cases within defined risk parameters); claims notification and first-step assessment (chatbot triage, automated data collection); compliance monitoring (automated NAICOM reporting, automated market conduct flag generation); and finance (automated premium reconciliation, investment portfolio reporting). The investment required: robotic process automation (RPA), workflow management systems, and API integration between core operational systems.

blocks.text: 27.8.2 Insurtech and the Nigerian Regulatory Sandbox

blocks.h: Insurtech (the application of technology to the insurance value chain, typically by startup companies with technology-first business models) is one of the most significant competitive dynamics in the Nigerian insurance market. Insurtech companies are challenging incumbent insurers in two dimensions simultaneously: distribution (by building direct digital customer relationships that bypass traditional agent and bancassurance channels) and risk analytics (by using alternative data sources, mobile money transaction patterns, agricultural satellite imagery, social media behaviour, to underwrite risks that incumbents cannot price).

NAICOM’s Insurtech Guidelines (August 2025) establish a regulatory sandbox framework: a controlled environment in which Insurtech entrants can test innovative insurance models under regulatory oversight before committing to full licensing. The sandbox framework enables NAICOM to engage with innovation without compromising the consumer protection standards that apply to fully licensed insurers. For incumbents, the sandbox is both a competitive threat intelligence source (providing early visibility into the Insurtech models NAICOM is engaging with) and a potential partnership opportunity (established insurers can partner with Insurtech sandbox participants to accelerate their own digital capabilities).

Nigerian incumbent life insurers face a strategic choice in responding to Insurtech disruption: build (develop their own digital capabilities from scratch), buy (acquire a promising Insurtech company), or partner (establish commercial distribution or technology partnerships with Insurtech companies while retaining the insurance risk on their own balance sheet). Each approach has different speed, cost, risk, and control implications.

The most commonly successful strategy for incumbents in comparable emerging insurance markets has been a hybrid approach: build the core digital customer-facing infrastructure (app, portal, digital distribution) from within, using the incumbent’s brand, data, and distribution relationships as competitive advantages; partner with Insurtech companies for specific capabilities (parametric product design, fraud detection AI, cooperative distribution technology) where the Insurtech’s specialist capability would take years to replicate internally.

blocks.text: 27.9.1 The Balanced Scorecard for Life Insurance

blocks.h: The Balanced Scorecard (BSC), developed by Robert Kaplan and David Norton, provides a multi-dimensional strategic performance measurement framework that translates strategy into measurable objectives across four perspectives: financial, customer, internal process, and learning and growth. The BSC corrects the dominant weakness of purely financial measurement systems (which capture only the financial results of past decisions) by also measuring the drivers of future financial performance.

blocks.text: 27.9.2 OKRs as a Complement to the Balanced Scorecard

blocks.h: Objectives and Key Results (OKRs), popularised by Google and widely adopted in technology companies, offer a complementary performance management framework to the BSC. Where the BSC provides the comprehensive strategic measurement architecture, OKRs provide a quarterly execution rhythm: each team sets 3–5 specific Objectives (ambitious, qualitative goals) with 3–5 Key Results per objective (specific, measurable outcomes that indicate the objective has been achieved). OKRs are designed to be ambitious (achieving 70% is considered success) and transparent (all teams’ OKRs are visible to the whole organisation).

For a Nigerian life insurer, OKRs are most useful for: driving specific strategic initiatives with clear short-term milestones (launching the digital distribution platform; completing the IFRS 17 implementation programme; achieving NAICOM’s Insurtech sandbox participation); and creating cross-functional alignment around shared outcomes (where the product team, the distribution team, and the technology team all share OKRs on the digital channel launch).

The risk that the insurer’s strategy is fundamentally flawed (it is built on incorrect assumptions about the market, consumer behaviour, or competitive dynamics) or that execution of the strategy is so poor that the strategic objectives are not achieved despite the strategy being sound. Strategic risk is distinct from operational risk (the risk of process failures) and from market risk (the risk of adverse financial market movements): it is the risk that the organisation is going in the wrong direction, or is unable to go in any direction effectively.

Strategic risks are among the most difficult to manage because they are often invisible until they have already materialised. The insurer that bet heavily on bancassurance distribution in 2020 and finds in 2025 that its key bank partner has launched its own insurance subsidiary did not have a bad strategy in 2020; the strategy became bad because the environment changed. Strategic risk management is not about predicting the future with certainty; it is about identifying the assumptions on which the strategy rests, monitoring those assumptions continuously, and having predefined responses when they are violated.

blocks.text: 27.10.2 Key Categories of Strategic Risk for Nigerian Life Insurers

items.h: Regulatory disruption risk: The risk that a regulatory change (a new NAICOM directive, a change in pension regulation, a change in tax treatment of insurance premiums) renders part of the insurer’s strategy non-viable. The most important mitigation is active regulatory monitoring and participation in the NAICOM consultation process; NAICOM’s regulatory changes rarely arrive without consultation, and insurers that engage in the consultation process have advance warning and influence over the shape of regulatory change.

Technology disruption risk: The risk that a new technology (AI underwriting, mobile-first distribution, parametric insurance platforms) creates a competitive asymmetry that the insurer cannot respond to quickly enough. The mitigation is not to try to predict which technology will dominate, but to build the organisational agility to adopt and integrate new technology rapidly when it proves commercially viable.

Distribution concentration risk: The risk that an insurer dependent on a single distribution channel (one bancassurance partner, one large broker, a small number of dominant agents) finds that channel disrupted or redirected. The mitigation is diversification of distribution channels and active management of the relationship with each significant intermediary.

Talent risk: The risk that the insurer lacks the strategic and technical leadership needed to execute its strategy. In the Nigerian insurance market, the talent pool for actuaries, investment professionals, digital specialists, and senior financial planners is limited. Talent risk is a binding constraint on many Nigerian insurers’ strategic ambitions.

Execution risk: The risk that a sound strategy is not executed effectively: the digital platform is built but not adopted; the new product is launched but not distributed; the new market is entered but not served with the quality required to build a sustainable customer base. Execution risk is managed through governance, project management discipline, and the OKR-style accountability mechanisms described above.

blocks.h: The Board’s Risk Committee is responsible for ensuring that the insurer’s strategic risks are identified, assessed, and managed within the risk appetite approved by the Board. The ORSA (described in Chapter 15) provides the annual structured assessment of the insurer’s risk profile, including strategic risks. But strategic risk governance cannot be limited to the annual ORSA cycle: strategic risks evolve continuously, and the Board must have a mechanism for monitoring strategic risk indicators between ORSA reports.

A strategic risk monitoring dashboard, reviewed quarterly by the Board Risk Committee, should track: the key assumptions underlying the strategic plan and the degree to which they remain valid; leading indicators of competitive disruption (Insurtech funding rounds, competitor product launches, bancassurance partnership changes); regulatory monitoring (NAICOM consultation documents, NIIRA 2025 implementation guidance); and strategic KPI trajectory (is the business on track against its multi-year strategic targets?).

blocks.text: 27.11 Building the Research Function in a Nigerian Life Insurer
27.11.1 The Research Function’s Mandate and Structure

blocks.h: A dedicated research function in a Nigerian life insurer is not a luxury; it is the intelligence infrastructure on which the strategy is built and continuously updated. Without a research function, the strategy team is reasoning from assumptions about consumer behaviour, competitor positioning, and market dynamics that are based on intuition, anecdote, and historical experience, none of which is a reliable guide to a market that is changing as rapidly as the Nigerian insurance market.

The research function’s mandate encompasses three domains: market intelligence (understanding the external environment, market size, competitive dynamics, regulatory trends); consumer insight (understanding the customer, their financial needs, their insurance attitudes, their product preferences, their complaints, and their advocacy behaviour); and operational analytics (using the insurer’s own data to generate insights on product performance, distribution productivity, claims patterns, and expense efficiency).

Head of Research and Strategy Insights
Sets the research agenda; commissions and oversees all major research programmes; presents insights to the Executive Committee and Board; owns the competitive intelligence function.
Strategic thinking; research methodology expertise; strong analytical and communication skills; insurance market knowledge.
Market Research Manager
Designs and executes primary consumer research programmes (surveys, focus groups, ethnographic studies); analyses and synthesises findings into actionable strategic recommendations.
Research design; survey methodology; qualitative analysis; data analysis; presentation skills.
Competitive Intelligence Analyst
Monitors competitor product launches, pricing, distribution investments, and financial results; tracks regulatory developments; maintains the competitive intelligence database.
Secondary research skills; analytical skills; insurance sector knowledge; ability to synthesise from multiple sources.
Data Analyst / BI Specialist

Designs and maintains the business intelligence dashboards used by the strategy, product, and distribution functions; builds models for churn prediction, lapse risk scoring, and market potential analysis.
SQL, Python or R; business intelligence tools (Tableau, Power BI); statistical modelling; insurance data literacy.
Product Research Specialist

Designs and executes the consumer research that informs product concept development; conducts product testing with target consumer panels; monitors product performance against the pilot and launch metrics.
Consumer research; product testing methodology; insurance product knowledge; qualitative and quantitative analysis.

blocks.h: The research function should maintain active access to the following data sources:

items.h: Internal data: The insurer’s own PAS (policy administration system) providing policy-level data on persistency, claims, and product performance; the CRM for distribution and customer interaction data; the finance system for product-level profitability data; the complaints register; and the agent performance data from the distribution management system.
EFInA and NBS surveys: Demand-side data on financial services access, insurance awareness, and household financial behaviour. Foundation data for market sizing and segmentation.
NAICOM regulatory data: Market-level premium income, claims statistics, and licensed insurer data from NAICOM’s published returns. Enables competitor benchmarking at the market level.

Third-party market research: Syndicated research from organisations such as FITCH Ratings, McKinsey, BCG, Swiss Re, Munich Re, and the GSMA on African insurance markets, financial inclusion trends, and digital distribution developments.
Regulatory monitoring: NAICOM consultation documents, NIIRA 2025 implementation guidance, PenCom regulatory communications, CBN policy statements, and FRC IFRS adoption guidance.

blocks.h: The most common failure mode of insurance research functions is the production of high-quality reports that sit in shared drives unread and unacted upon. Research that does not change decisions is not research; it is documentation. Building a research culture that produces strategic impact requires:

items.h: Co-creation with decision-makers: The research agenda should be designed around the questions that the CEO, CFO, CMO, and Chief Distribution Officer actually need answered to make their most important current decisions. Research conducted without this grounding tends to answer interesting questions rather than urgent ones.

Decision-ready formats: Research outputs should be presented in a format that enables decision-making: a one-page insight summary with a clear ‘so what?’ and a recommended action, backed by the full data in an appendix. A 60-page research report that requires two hours of reading before a strategic conclusion can be drawn will not change decisions; a two-page executive summary with three actionable recommendations will.

Research governance: A regular research-to-strategy review: a monthly meeting between the research function and the strategy, product, and distribution teams at which new research findings are shared, interpreted, and translated into specific management actions with owners and deadlines.

blocks.text: 27.12 Advisory: The Strategy and Research Investment Agenda

blocks.h: The Nigerian life insurer that will define the next decade of the market is not the one with the most agents or the largest existing customer base. It is the one that makes the most strategically coherent choices about which customers to serve, builds the digital infrastructure to serve them cost-effectively, generates the consumer insights to serve them relevantly, and executes with the management discipline to translate strategic intent into operational reality.

blocks.title: Advisory: Five Strategic Investment Priorities for a Competitive Nigerian Life Insurer in the Post-NIIRA 2025 Era

blocks.h: PRIORITY 1: CHOOSE A POSITION AND COMMIT TO IT. The most expensive strategic mistake a Nigerian life insurer can make is to spread its investment across all customer segments, all distribution channels, and all product lines, achieving mediocrity everywhere. Choose the customer segment in which the insurer can be genuinely excellent (mass market digital, corporate EB, HNI advisory, or microinsurance community) and invest in the capabilities that position requires at a level that creates genuine competitive differentiation.

PRIORITY 2: BUILD THE DIGITAL INFRASTRUCTURE NOW. The window for building digital distribution infrastructure before it becomes table stakes is closing. An insurer that deploys a robust digital distribution platform, a customer-facing mobile app, and a USSD enrolment system in 2025–2026 will have three to five years of operational experience and consumer data ahead of a competitor that begins the investment in 2029. Digital infrastructure is a compounding asset, the data it generates improves risk pricing, fraud detection, and customer service with every additional year of operation.

PRIORITY 3: INVEST IN CONSUMER INSIGHT. The trust deficit that holds back the Nigerian insurance market is, at its core, an insight problem: insurers do not know what consumers actually need, what they actually fear, and what would actually persuade them to purchase and retain insurance. A ₦50–80 million annual research programme, a small fraction of the marketing budget, that generates granular consumer insight across the target segments is the highest-return intelligence investment available.

PRIORITY 4: BUILD TALENT FOR THE STRATEGY THE INSURER IS TRYING TO EXECUTE. A digital-first strategy requires digital talent: product managers with fintech experience, data scientists who understand insurance, UX designers who understand low-income Nigerian users. A corporate EB strategy requires employee benefit specialists with CIIN Associateship and retirement planning expertise. Talent acquisition and development must be the leading investment in the strategic plan, not the lagging one.

PRIORITY 5: TREAT NIIRA 2025 COMPLIANCE AS A COMPETITIVE ADVANTAGE, NOT A COST. Insurers that achieve genuine compliance excellence (not minimum-level compliance but the cultural, governance, and operational quality that NIIRA 2025 mandates at its best) will be trusted by NAICOM, trusted by brokers and corporate buyers, and trusted by policyholders in a way that rivals scrambling to meet minimum requirements cannot match. In a trust-deficit market, regulatory credibility is a marketing asset.

blocks.title: A Final Note: The Insurer That Earns the Right to Grow

blocks.h: Nigeria’s insurance market is one of the most significant untapped financial services opportunities in the world. The combination of a massive, young, increasingly digitally connected population; a regulatory framework that is maturing toward international standards; a mandatory insurance architecture that creates structural premium floors; and a deep cultural value of family and community protection creates the conditions for sustained, high-quality insurance market growth.

But this growth is not automatic, and it will not be distributed evenly. It will accrue to the insurers that: pay claims promptly and fairly, building the trust that makes their brand a referral engine; build distribution infrastructure that reaches consumers where they are, not where it is convenient for the insurer; design products that genuinely address consumer needs, not actuarial convenience; invest in the talent and governance required by NIIRA 2025; and have the strategic discipline to make choices rather than to pursue every opportunity simultaneously. The insurer that earns the right to grow does so by being genuinely excellent at the things that matter most to the people it serves.

The set of deliberate choices an organisation makes about which customers to serve, which products to offer, which distribution channels to invest in, and which capabilities to build, creating a distinctive and defensible competitive position.

A structured environmental scanning framework analysing Political, Economic, Social, Technological, Environmental, and Legal forces in the macro-environment that create opportunities and threats for the organisation.

A framework for analysing competitive dynamics in an industry through five structural forces: threat of new entrants, bargaining power of buyers, bargaining power of suppliers, threat of substitutes, and intensity of competitive rivalry.
A competitive strategy based on having the lowest cost base in the market, enabling competitive pricing and superior margins at market-rate premiums.
A competitive strategy based on offering products or services that customers recognise as distinctively superior to alternatives and are willing to pay a premium for.
A competitive strategy targeting a specific niche market with either lower cost or superior differentiation relative to broader competitors.
A deep understanding of consumer behaviour, attitudes, barriers, and motivations, derived from structured market research, that informs product development, marketing, and strategy.

The structured, gate-based process through which a life insurer transforms consumer insight and market opportunity into a commercially viable, actuarially sound, and regulatorily compliant new product.

The application of technology (typically by startup companies) to the insurance value chain, including digital distribution, AI-powered underwriting, parametric insurance platforms, and data analytics.
A controlled regulatory environment in which Insurtech entrants can test innovative insurance models under NAICOM supervision before committing to full licensing, established under NIIRA 2025.
A strategic performance measurement framework translating strategy into measurable objectives across four perspectives: financial, customer, internal process, and learning and growth.
A goal-setting framework in which teams define ambitious qualitative Objectives and specific measurable Key Results, used as a quarterly execution rhythm complementing the Balanced Scorecard.
The risk that the insurer’s strategy is fundamentally flawed or that execution is so poor that strategic objectives are not achieved, distinct from operational risk and financial market risk.
The organisational unit responsible for generating the market intelligence, consumer insights, and operational analytics that inform strategic and product decisions in a life insurance company.
Systematic monitoring and analysis of competitor products, pricing, distribution investments, and financial performance to inform strategic positioning decisions.

A business strategy that uses technology as its primary enabler, defining how digital tools will transform customer acquisition, policyholder servicing, risk assessment, and claims management to improve competitive position.

items.h: Porter, M.E. Competitive Strategy: Techniques for Analyzing Industries and Competitors (Free Press, 1980). The foundational text for Five Forces and generic competitive strategies; directly applicable to insurance market analysis.

Porter, M.E. Competitive Advantage: Creating and Sustaining Superior Performance (Free Press, 1985). The value chain framework and the detailed mechanics of cost leadership, differentiation, and focus.

Kaplan, R.S. and Norton, D.P. The Balanced Scorecard: Translating Strategy into Action (Harvard Business School Press, 1996). The definitive Balanced Scorecard reference; insurance-specific applications are available from the Balanced Scorecard Institute.

Johnson, G., Whittington, R., Scholes, K., Angwin, D., and Rägnvaldur, R. Exploring Strategy (12th edn, Pearson, 2020). Comprehensive strategic management text including PESTEL, Five Forces, and strategic risk.

EFInA. Access to Financial Services in Nigeria Survey. efina.org.ng. The most authoritative consumer demand-side data for Nigerian insurance market research.
GSMA. State of the Industry Report on Mobile Money. gsma.com. Annual benchmark for mobile money and digital financial services penetration; essential for digital strategy calibration.
